title: Scientists Rinsed Out Baby Sharks' Stomachs and Found Songbirds

scenes.text: Baby tiger sharks eat woodpeckers. Out at sea.
In 2010, a small tiger shark hauled onto a research boat in the Gulf of Mexico threw up a ball of feathers. They came from a brown thrasher, a backyard songbird.
So for eight years, scientists flushed out the stomachs of 105 tiger sharks. Forty-one had eaten birds.
Eleven species. Sparrows, wrens, doves, swallows. Not one seagull, not one pelican.
About two billion birds cross the Gulf every year. In autumn, storms knock the exhausted ones into the water.
And autumn is exactly when newborn tiger sharks, about three feet long, crowd that coast. The birds fall. The babies are underneath.

description:
Baby tiger sharks in the Gulf of Mexico eat songbirds.
Over eight years, researchers led by Marcus Drymon of Mississippi State University flushed the stomachs of 105 tiger sharks and found bird remains in 41 of them; DNA tests at the Field Museum identified 11 species of land birds, including wrens, swallows, sparrows, sapsuckers and doves, and no seabirds at all. The birds are thought to fall into the sea during autumn storms on migration, when young tiger sharks are most abundant off Mississippi and Alabama. The study was published in the journal Ecology in 2019.
What's the strangest thing you've heard of a shark eating?
subject: tiger shark
first_comment: One idea from the study: tiger shark mothers may give birth in the northern Gulf because the falling songbirds make an easy first meal. Clever, or just lucky?
